name: Asilulu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Collins, James T. 2003, Asilulu-English Dictionary (NUSA/Universitas Katolik Atma Jaya, Jakarta; xlii+209pp, with phonological front matter)

new_statements.quote: There are two additional symbols. The colon (:) marks long vowels, which contrast phonemically with short vowels. The stress mark (´) is used to mark words in which stress does not fall on the penultimate syllable. [...] These sequences do not constitute diphthongs, of which there are none in Asilulu. Consequently, when such a sequence occurs at the end of a word, unless otherwised marked, stress always falls on the penultimate syllable, that is the first vowel of the sequence. Similarly, when long vowels (i:, e:, a:, u:, o:) appear at the end of a word, stress falls on that vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (root) word by default; every vowel counts as a syllable (there are no diphthongs), so a word-final vowel sequence is stressed on its first vowel, and a word-final long vowel is stressed (Collins treats V: as equivalent to VV, fn 29). Words whose stress is not penultimate are lexically marked with an acute accent in the dictionary (e.g. harám 'forbidden', an Arabic loan, p. 18). Pronominal clitics attached to a word do not move its stress (p. xxviii: 'the addition of clitic pronominal markers does not affect the original stress of the cliticized word'; [ratakeru] keeps the stress of ratak), which is also the point of Collins 1983 p. 82: Asilulu stress stays on the penult of the root under suffixation, unlike the Hoamoal languages where it shifts.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with non-penultimate stress exist and are marked with the stress mark in the dictionary; the marked headwords seen are loanwords with final stress (harám, from Arabic). Word-final long vowels take the stress. Cliticized/suffixed words keep root stress, so surface stress can be antepenultimate or earlier in such forms (Collins 1983 p. 82: húlane, ʔúlule, ráwaʔe, palaʔékni).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (dictionary headwords, citation forms); the clitic remark concerns host+pronominal-clitic words. No phrase-level or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 2003 describes the Asilulu of Asilulu village proper (Nuclear Asilulu); he notes three dialects (Asilulu, Ureng, Hena Lima/Negeri Lima) and that the fricative r is a village-level marker. No separate dialect glottocodes involved; the statement is for asil1242 as a whole.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU. ix+168 pp.
sources.note: p. 82 (PDF p. 92): 'An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress.' Examples Asilulu húlane 'moon', ʔúlule 'kind of fruit', ráwaʔe 'tomorrow' vs Luhu hulané etc.; Asilulu palaʔékni 'recall him'.
